title: What CoFlow does
description: CoFlow keeps your team’s engineering standards in one reviewed place, gives them to coding agents for each task and checks the result.
text: In one paragraph CoFlow holds the rules your team expects code to follow, the facts agents keep needing about your system, and the lessons your team learns from reviews, corrections and incidents. It gives coding agents the rules that apply to the files they are about to change, reviews pull requests against the same rules, and runs review agents whose actions people approve. People decide what becomes a rule. No agent can merge, approve a pull request, push or bypass a check. How the pieces fit Start from the starter rule packs that match your stack. coflow init picks them from your manifests. Connect your coding agents. They read the rules through their own rule files and the CoFlow MCP server. Review changes. coflow check runs locally; the hosted service reviews pull requests. Capture what goes wrong: review findings, corrections in agent sessions, reverts, tickets and production incidents. The lessons pipeline turns repeated evidence into rule proposals. A person reviews each one; a pull request makes it active. Watch the scorecard, the cost ledger and the evaluation runs to see whether the rules help. Where to go next Quickstart Install the CLI, initialize a repository and connect a coding agent. Starter library What the starter packs cover and how your own rules take over. Review and tool checks What runs locally, what runs on the hosted worker and what “not run” means. Agent Studio Seventeen agent templates, the autonomy ladder and approvals. Security Tenant isolation, roles, approvals and agent limits. Plans and billing The planned launch plans, trial and credits. Availability CoFlow is in private build. These guides describe the pilot release. Some features work only after an operator configures them, and some are not ready yet. The feature status page lists which is which. Publishing documentation does not turn on a feature in your workspace. Ask about the pilot .

title: Quickstart
description: Put your team’s standards in front of a coding agent, check a change and see a rule proposal, on your own repository.
text: Install the CLI The local workflow needs no account, no server and no model key. CoFlow is a Python package with a coflow command. Install it into its own virtual environment from the source your onboarding contact gives you, then check that the command works: python3 -m venv ~/coflow-env ~/coflow-env/bin/pip install <package source from onboarding> export PATH="$HOME/coflow-env/bin:$PATH" coflow --help coflow --help lists init , validate , scan , compile , export , check , inbox and the other commands. The commands are written for macOS and Linux. Initialize a repository cd ~/src/your-repo coflow init coflow validate coflow compile --paths app/main.py init reads your manifests (for example pyproject.toml , package.json or alembic.ini ), prints the packs it chose, copies them to .coflow/rules/ , writes .coflow/config.yaml and generates AGENTS.md , the Copilot instructions, the Cursor rules and the agent skills. Choose packs yourself with --packs , or a named set with --bundle . compile prints the rules an agent gets for that path, cut to the token budget. Commit .coflow/ and the generated files so the whole team gets them. Connect your coding agent coflow connect claude --dry-run coflow connect claude Name your client: claude , cursor , vscode (GitHub Copilot), codex , gemini , windsurf , cline , zed , jetbrains , amazonq , roo or aider . coflow connect --all connects every client whose own files are already in the repository. --dry-run prints the diff of each file first. connect writes the client’s rule files and merges a coflow server into the client’s project MCP file, keeping every other server there. Windsurf, Cline and Zed keep MCP servers in a user-level file, so for them it prints the entry to paste. Aider has no MCP client and gets rule files only. The local MCP server needs no token. To use the hosted service instead, add --hosted ; the client then reads your credential from the COFLOW_API_TOKEN environment variable, which you set in your shell. connect never writes a token into a file. See coding agents and MCP server and CLI . What the agent gets The local server offers fifteen tools: five rule tools, eight context tools, get_budget and record_cost . The ones to start with: get_standards : the rules for the files of the task, ordered and cut to a token budget. get_rule : the full text of one rule, with its examples. record_outcome : the agent reports whether it followed a rule. propose_rule : the agent proposes a rule. It lands in .coflow/proposals/ and does nothing until a person merges it. where_is and remember : facts about your system the agent looked up once. Tell the agent once: “Before you change code, call get_standards for the files you will touch.” Check a change git diff | coflow check --diff - Exit code 0 means clean and 1 means a required rule is broken. With --strict , exit code 2 means a rule in scope had no check run. A rule enforced by a tool that is not installed is reported as not run, never as passed. Rules that need a model review are listed as “not reviewed (no model)” until you configure a model. See a rule proposal Correct the agent in a session, for example “always pass a timeout to requests calls”. When it agrees the correction is a standing rule, it calls propose_rule and a file appears in .coflow/proposals/ . You can also capture corrections: coflow connect claude --capture (or cursor , gemini ) installs the client’s end-of-session hook. For other clients, record one yourself with coflow lesson "always pass a timeout to requests calls" . coflow inbox lists what was captured. A proposal is never active. A person reviews it and merges the rule file in a pull request. Run coflow export after that so the agent files carry the new rule. Next steps coflow scan shows the detected tools and the packs it proposes. coflow context setup writes five questions about your system for a person to answer once. The hosted service adds pull request review, the approvals inbox, Agent Studio and chat approvals. See Connect and Agent Studio .

title: Feature status
description: What ships in the pilot release, what works once an operator configures it, and what is not ready.
text: Shipped in the pilot release This code is on the pilot release branch and runs without extra provider setup: The coflow CLI and the local MCP server: init , scan , compile , export , check , connect for 12 coding agents, lesson , inbox , context , search , eval , cost , evidence-pack and the others. The starter rule packs, starter bundles, stack detection and the generated agent files. Local review with 13 linter and scanner adapters (each runs when it is installed) and host checks. The lessons pipeline, rule proposals and approval policies with reviewer groups. The hosted API, the approvals inbox, and Agent Studio with 17 agent templates seeded at shadow. Organization-owned CoFlow tables under forced row-level security. The scorecard, the cost ledger, the evaluation datasets and harness, and the compliance evidence pack. Works once configured These are in the release but do nothing until an operator sets them up for your organization: Pull request review on GitHub: needs the GitHub App or the Nango connection. An operator must confirm a GitHub App installation before it routes anything. GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud review: each host is turned on separately. The hosted MCP service: off by default, and requires agent credentials. Agent Studio runs on real pull requests: start once your organization binds an agent to a repository. Model-backed review: rules that need a model stay “not reviewed (no model)” until a model is configured. Slack and Microsoft Teams approvals: need the chat app installed for your workspace. Production evidence from Datadog, Sentry, PagerDuty, Opsgenie and CloudWatch: needs a source configuration with credential references. Scheduled work (weekly scorecard, nightly host snapshots, approval escalation and expiry, ops ingest, agent schedules): nothing runs on a schedule until an operator creates the jobs. See scheduled jobs . Not ready yet Do not plan a pilot around these: Opening a ticket from an agent: no Jira or Linear connection for agent tickets ships yet. An approved ticket action fails with a note that says so, and nothing is sent. Proposal pull requests: an agent’s proposal pull request adds one file under .coflow/proposals/ , is always a draft and never changes rules. Approving on the Proposals screen returns the rule file text and does not open a pull request. Agent Studio runs on GitLab and Bitbucket: studio agent runs are GitHub only in this release. The other hosts get the plain review. Tool checks on the hosted worker: the worker image installs ruff, bandit, zizmor, actionlint and hadolint, and runs them only on files it can rebuild whole from the patch (new files, or patches that start at line 1). Every other tool check on the server is reported as not run. See review and tool checks . Hosted MCP: accepts organization-wide agent credentials only; a credential bound to a project is refused. Call budgets are kept per process, so run one instance. Repository access inside an organization: repositories are not tied to workspace projects yet, so any member can read any repository’s CoFlow records in their organization. Some scorecard metrics on a fresh pilot: reviewer agreement needs 20 findings with a disposition, and repeat rate needs evidence linked to a rule. The scorecard says “not measured” with the reason. The server’s detected system map is whatever coflow sync last posted, and the server flags stale facts by age only. Screens not built yet: chat settings, rule sync grants, host snapshots, decision history and evidence on its own. Their routes exist. Live accounts: the GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket integrations were built and tested against recorded fakes, not against live accounts. Treat the first repository on each host as a test. The same applies to the other vendor integrations; see Connect . Promotion above shadow: the proposed precision and recall thresholds have not been validated against a hosted model or real pull requests. Billing: the plans, trial and credits on plans and billing are the planned launch model and are not live. Confirm your workspace Ask during onboarding for the deployed version, the integrations configured for your organization, your sign-in URL and your role. Use your workspace and its release evidence, not the examples on this website, to decide what is live.

title: Plans, trial and billing
description: Two plans priced per developer seat, a 14-day trial and monthly credits for model and compute-heavy work.
text: Status Planned launch billing model. This page describes the billing model being built for launch. It is not live: CoFlow is in private build, nothing on this website takes payment, and the values below are proposed starting values that may change before launch. Two plans CoFlow is priced per developer seat, billed monthly or annually. There are two plans: Plan Seat price Included credits What it adds Team To be confirmed 1,000 per seat per month Starter rule packs and your own rules, compiled context, the MCP server and CLI, review, the lessons pipeline, Agent Studio and approvals Business To be confirmed 3,000 per seat per month Everything in Team, plus single sign-on (SSO) and SOC 2 Type II audit support Seat prices and the discount for annual billing are to be confirmed. Prices will be in US dollars and exclude tax. 14-day free trial The trial lasts 14 days and includes 2,000 credits for the organization. A payment card is required to start the trial. At the end of the trial it converts to a paid subscription on the plan you chose, unless you cancel before then. Business security Business includes single sign-on and SOC 2 Type II audit support. Single sign-on needs identity configuration for your organization. Audit support covers readiness and evidence workflows, such as the compliance evidence pack . These docs do not assert that CoFlow holds an issued SOC 2 Type II report. Read organizations, roles and approvals and RLS and tenant isolation . Credits in brief Credits pay for model and compute-heavy work: evaluations, lesson drafting and testing, agent sandbox, shadow and live runs, and model-backed review. Rules, compiled context, the MCP server, host checks and linters never use credits. Monthly credits do not roll over. Credit packs add more. Details are on credits and usage . During the private build Pilot terms are agreed with each team directly. The website prepares an enquiry email; it does not sell plans, start trials or take card details. Talk to us about the pilot .

title: Credits and usage
description: What credits pay for, what never uses them, credit packs and how usage is shown.
text: Status Planned launch billing model. This page describes the billing model being built for launch. It is not live: CoFlow is in private build, nothing on this website takes payment, and the values below are proposed starting values that may change before launch. What credits pay for Evaluations: harness and dataset runs that call a model. Lessons: drafting rule proposals from evidence and testing them. Agent runs: sandbox, shadow and live runs in Agent Studio. Model-backed review: review steps that need a model. What never uses credits Deterministic features never use credits and keep working when the balance is zero: rules and rule packs, compiled context, the MCP server, host checks, and the linters and scanners CoFlow runs. Monthly allowance Credits Team 1,000 per seat per month Business 3,000 per seat per month Trial 2,000 per organization Monthly credits do not roll over to the next month. Credit packs One credit is worth $0.01. Packs add credits on top of the monthly allowance: Pack Credits $50 5,000 $200 20,000 $1,000 100,000 Pack credits expire 12 months after purchase. Auto top-up is optional. When it is on, it buys a pack when the balance runs low, up to a monthly cap you set. How a run is charged Cost before the run: CoFlow shows what a run will cost and reserves the credits before it starts. Failed runs: credits for a run that fails are refunded. Low balance: when the balance cannot cover a run, the run is refused rather than started and left half done. Seeing your usage A usage meter in the app shows the balance and what has been used this month. The Usage page breaks usage down and exports it as CSV. Credits are separate from the cost ledger , which records the tokens and runner minutes your own coding agents and models use, priced with your own contract prices. Your coding-agent subscriptions are also separate.

title: Starter library and rule packs
description: The packs a team starts with, before CoFlow learns its own rules from its code, reviews and tickets.
text: A starting point, not the rulebook CoFlow ships a starter library of 400+ rules in 33 packs. It is what a team begins with. Once CoFlow scans your repositories, reviews your pull requests, reads your tickets and incidents and connects to your tools, the rules your team learns from its own code and corrections, approved by people, become the main rulebook. The starter packs fill the gaps and can be tuned or retired. What the packs cover Security: web application security, access and secrets, supply chain and dependency pinning, and tenant isolation. Testing: what each kind of change should come with, coverage of changed lines, flaky tests and test data. Accessibility: frontend accessibility, mapped to WCAG 2.2 success criteria. Languages and stacks: Python, TypeScript, C and C++, firmware, web and frontend frameworks, ORMs and migrations, SQL, containers, CI workflows, logging and observability. Compliance frameworks: change control and access rules mapped to control identifiers in SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and security rules mapped to OWASP, CWE and NIST SSDF. Field packs: general engineering rules learned by running a multi-tenant AI product, covering database tenant isolation, caches, background workers, search indexes, model calls, evaluation runs, deploys, CI cost and how coding agents work. Starter bundles A bundle installs a named set of packs in one step: saas-multitenant : a multi-tenant web service with a relational database, background workers and CI. ai-product : the multi-tenant set plus packs for model calls, evaluation and search indexes. agent-team : the smallest set, for a team whose changes are mostly written by coding agents. coflow init --bundle saas-multitenant The first two also add the packs that stack detection proposes for the repository. coflow scan shows what was detected. Rules scoped to a framework load only when detection finds that framework. Evidence bands Rules in the field packs can carry an evidence band: very common, common or occasional. A band says how often the fault the rule prevents was seen in the history the rule came from. Use bands to decide which rules to trial first. A band is not severity, and another team’s faults will be distributed differently. Verification status The identifiers the packs cite (control numbers, weakness numbers and linter rule codes) were each checked against public sources, and the result is recorded per identifier. A build check fails when a rule cites an identifier the record does not hold. A mapping says a rule is relevant to the subject of a control. It does not certify that any control is met. The packs hold identifiers and CoFlow’s own wording; no licensed standard text was copied. An auditor may scope a control differently. Tuning the starter rules Start advisory. Set installed rules to advisory in your copy under .coflow/rules/ unless your team already enforces them, and read the findings for two or three weeks. Promote with your own evidence. Make a rule required when your reviews, failed checks or incidents show the fault it prevents, and record the reason in the pull request. Record deviations. Where a rule conflicts with a constraint of your system, record a deviation with a reason and an expiry instead of ignoring the finding. Retire what does not fit. A rule that never matches, or whose findings are dismissed, can be retired in your copy. Change team numbers. Settings such as the coverage minimum for changed lines (80 percent by default) are team defaults, not facts.

title: Rules, lessons and human review
description: How evidence becomes a proposal, and how a person turns a proposal into a rule.
text: Rules live in your repository A rule is a file under .coflow/rules/ , versioned with your code. It names where it applies, how it is checked, its severity and its examples. coflow sync posts the repository’s rules to the hosted service so server review and the hosted MCP server use the same set. Where lessons come from Review findings and how people disposed of them. Failed checks, reverts and fixes of earlier fixes. Tickets in Jira or Linear, and production incidents and error groups from your monitoring tools. Corrections people make in coding-agent sessions, captured by a session-end hook or recorded with coflow lesson . The lessons pipeline The pipeline classifies evidence, clusters related items, drafts a rule, checks it against existing rules so a lesson is stored once, and opens a proposal with its evidence attached. Before any of that, secrets are dropped, identifiers are replaced and instruction-like text is neutralized. Mined text is data, never instructions. Drafting and testing a lesson with a model are credit-using work under the planned billing model . Human review A proposal is never active. A person reviews it, and the rule takes effect when its pull request is merged. Approval policies cover new rules, rule changes, retirements and deviations. Each names its reviewers and approvers and how many of each are needed. The person who proposed a rule cannot approve it while another eligible reviewer exists. A proposal made by an agent counts as proposed by the member who created the agent’s credential. If the author is the only eligible reviewer, the record says “approved by the only eligible reviewer” and marks independence as not met. Reviewers can decide in the app or on a Slack or Teams card. A chat decision is recorded; the rule still becomes active only when its pull request merges. See organizations, roles and approvals for policies, quorum and independence. Rules and facts are different A rule constrains behavior and takes effect only after a person approves it. A fact about your project, such as where a database is or how to run a service, is remembered as soon as an agent learns it. See project memory .

title: Compiled context and budgets
description: Give an agent the rules for the files it will touch, within a token budget that is never exceeded silently.
text: How rules are selected Rules are matched to a task by the paths it touches and by the languages and frameworks detected in the repository. coflow compile --paths prints the result. Through MCP, get_standards does the same and takes an optional description of the task, which ranks the most relevant rules first within each severity. Budgets Advisory and informational rules are dropped first. When the required rules alone are over the budget, their statements are shortened to one sentence. If that is still too much, the lowest-ranked required rules are listed by name only, and get_rule returns their full text. The response says which rules were shortened, deferred or dropped. Compiled context is deterministic and never uses credits. Agent files Files every session loads, such as AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md , carry only the rules that apply to every file. Rules scoped to paths, languages or frameworks reach the agent through skills, Cursor rules, path-scoped Copilot files and get_standards . coflow export --check exits 1 when a generated file no longer matches the rules. Measuring context cost Each compile can be recorded in the cost ledger as the tokens of the rules an agent was given, and the scorecard reports context cost. Size estimates are not a published savings figure. Measure your agents’ real token use and retries separately. Instruction packages in the platform API The platform API also compiles persisted instruction packages with selection reasons and pinned dependencies ( POST /v1/instructions/compile , reopened with GET /v1/instructions/{id} ). A historical package keeps its original content. Declared conflicts, missing approved dependencies or required content over the budget block a package.

title: Project memory: facts learned once
description: Facts about your system that an agent looks up once, so no later session has to find them again.
text: Three layers Declared: .coflow/context/system.yaml , verified entries changed through a pull request. Learned: .coflow/context/learned.yaml , facts agents stored with remember , marked unverified and capped at 300. Detected: computed from your files on each read and never stored. Reads merge the layers in that order of trust, and every answer names the layer it came from. The system map The system map describes services, datastores, data flows, environments, external systems, a glossary and conventions. Agents ask where_is , get the context for the paths they touch, and check the impact of a change. How facts are learned and corrected A fact learned twice by different sessions gains a confirmation. A fact that contradicts an earlier one is kept beside it, newest first, and flagged for a person. Agents can correct and forget facts. coflow context stale lists facts that may be out of date. promote writes one proposal for many facts. A person reviews it and accept moves them into the declared layer as verified. Playbooks Playbooks tell agents when to use another system (observability, cloud, issue tracker) and how, with read-only queries. coflow context setup runs detection, installs the playbooks whose systems exist and writes five questions for a person to answer once. Credentials and the server No context file stores a credential value, only a reference naming where it lives. On the hosted service, the detected layer is whatever coflow sync last posted, and a scheduled job flags learned facts that are unverified, unconfirmed and older than 90 days.

title: Structured review and tool checks
description: How CoFlow reviews a change, which tools run where, and why “not run” is never a pass.
text: How a review works The review engine parses the diff, finds the rules in scope for each changed file and runs each rule’s checks. A rule can be checked by a linter or scanner, by a host check on repository settings and pull request facts, or by a model review. Findings name the rule they come from. The same engine serves coflow check , the server’s pull request review, rule tests and evaluations. “Not run” is never a pass A tool that is missing, turned off, times out, exits unexpectedly or cannot parse a file is reported as not run with the reason. Rules that need a model are “not reviewed (no model)” until one is configured. A host setting CoFlow cannot read is reported as unknown. None of these count as passing. Tool adapters CoFlow has adapters for 13 tools. Locally, each runs when it is installed. On the hosted worker, this release installs five of them: Tool Reads Locally Hosted worker ruff Python When installed Yes bandit Python When installed Yes zizmor GitHub Actions workflows When installed Yes actionlint GitHub Actions workflows When installed Yes hadolint Dockerfiles When installed Yes eslint JavaScript and TypeScript When installed Not installed gitleaks Added lines in any file When installed Not installed semgrep Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, YAML, Dockerfiles, shell When installed Not installed sqlfluff SQL When installed Not installed squawk SQL migrations When installed Not installed mypy Python When installed, with a mypy configuration Never (no checkout) cppcheck C and C++ When installed, with a compile database Never (no checkout) clang-tidy C and C++ When installed, with a compile database Never (no checkout) On the hosted worker, tools run only on files the worker can rebuild whole from the patch: new files, or patches that start at line 1. Other files are reported as not run. coflow tools lists the adapters, the version found on your machine and how many rules each serves. Tools a pack names without an adapter, such as a compiler, CodeQL, Trivy or pytest, are reported as not run by coflow check . What an adapter promises It never executes project code. Files are copied into a fresh temporary directory, and configuration that can load code (such as ESLint config modules or mypy plugins) is never read from the repository. It runs with a minimal environment. No credential from the caller reaches the tool. Time, output, file count and file size are bounded. A tool binary inside the repository being checked is skipped, so a pull request cannot supply its own linter. The server reads tool settings at the pull request’s base commit, so a pull request cannot turn a check off for itself. Host checks Host checks read repository settings and pull request facts from the code host: A pull request is required, and approvals are required. An approval covers the final commit. Required status checks are set and passed. Force pushes are blocked and protection applies to administrators. No agent merged the pull request. Where a host has no matching setting, the check reports “not available” with status unknown. Host checks never use credits. Model-backed review Rules whose checks need judgment use a model review when your organization configures a model. Under the planned billing model , model-backed review uses credits; tool and host checks do not.

title: Testing requirements
description: What a change should come with, and the agents and contracts that check it.
text: What the testing rules cover The testing starter pack says what each kind of change should come with: tests for new routes, functions and migrations, coverage of changed lines, handling of flaky tests, fixtures built from the real schema, data policy tests run as the restricted runtime role, and verification notes in the pull request. Field packs add CI checks that catch import, collection and migration faults cheaply, and frontend component and end-to-end test practice. The coverage minimum for changed lines is a team setting (80 percent by default). Change it in your configuration. Agents that check tests test-guard : reviews test changes for network use and production data, and reports files no check or rule covers. test-writer : proposes the tests a changed function, route or migration is missing, as a draft comment with a sketch. It never commits code. incident-follow-up : checks that a revert, a fix of a fix or an incident fix comes with a regression test and a recorded lesson. pr-describer : checks that a pull request says how it was verified. See Agent Studio . Acceptance contracts Specifications capture requirements, positive and negative checks and source references in immutable revisions. Approval checks the expected revision and is recorded under a different person. A specification compiled with a code commit binds the acceptance contract into the instruction package. Required checks run in your development or verification environment. Clients submit pass, fail or skipped with evidence. Skipped checks do not count as passes, and submitted results are reported by the client, not independently executed by CoFlow.

title: Evaluations and harness
description: Measure a reviewer or a rule on a pinned dataset before you trust it with more autonomy.
text: The harness The harness tests a rule on its examples, runs a regression suite, replays a task and checks release gates. Every run is saved as a record pinned to the dataset version, engine and settings it used, so two runs can be compared. Datasets Datasets are original and synthetic: the code belongs to an invented shop service, with no customer code, names or records. There is one dataset per review agent with 20 or more cases, plus a core review set, a security set, a lessons set and an adherence set. Cases include violations, clean changes that look risky, near misses a linter does not flag, defects only on deleted lines, files outside a rule’s scope and generated files. Secrets in cases are fake and shaped to be recognized as fake. Running an evaluation coflow eval run review-core coflow eval run security-monitor --tools all A run is compared with the committed baseline. The default tool set is ruff alone, so baselines stay comparable across machines; a baseline records the tool set it was taken with, and runs with another tool set are compared only with a matching baseline. Reading the results honestly Linters alone reach a minority of expected findings. In the core review set, the tools find 11 of 39 expected findings; in the security set they find no missing authorization, no missing tenant scope and no request forgery. Those findings need a model review. Each agent template carries proposed precision and recall thresholds. They are starting values and have not been validated against a hosted model or real pull requests. Runs with linters alone do not meet them, so promotion above shadow needs a model-backed run. Evaluations and promotion Promoting an agent to assist or auto needs a regression run on the agent’s own dataset whose precision and recall meet its thresholds. A partial run, or a run on another dataset, is refused. See Agent Studio . Adding cases Add a case from a real incident by writing a sanitized, synthetic version of the change that caused it. Under the planned billing model , evaluations that call a model use credits.

title: Scorecard and cost
description: Whether the rules are loaded, followed and worth what they cost.
text: The scorecard The scorecard reports nine metrics in four groups: Group Metrics Control Coverage, override rate Adherence Adherence rate, first-pass adherence, repeat rate Evaluation Reviewer agreement, time to rule Optimization Context cost, dead rules A metric without enough data says “not measured” and why. Reviewer agreement needs 20 findings with a disposition; a rule counts as dead after 90 days without a match. When a rule is missed, the cause points to the fix: not loaded (fix its scope), unclear (rewrite it), ignored (enforce it more strongly) or wrong (retire it). A scheduled job can post the weekly scorecard to chat. The cost ledger The ledger records quantities, never prices: input, output and cached tokens, model calls and CI runner minutes, tagged with repository, agent, pack, workflow and pull request. You enter prices from your own contracts. A record without a price is reported as unknown, never as zero. coflow cost report gives spend per merged pull request, per review, per accepted finding and per approved rule, and the share of spend that produced nothing, such as cancelled runs or rules loaded in every session that never matched. Budgets Budgets apply per organization, repository or agent, per day or month. Before spending, an agent asks for a decision: Allow: within budget. Degrade: past the warning line; take the cheaper path. Stop: over budget. The work ends and is reported as partial. A stop never passes a required check. Savings are tested first coflow cost advise lists proposed savings, each with its evidence and arithmetic. A saving is adopted only when a harness run on the same pinned dataset shows quality holds: pass rate does not drop, no passing case fails and review time rises by at most 10 percent. Fewer than 20 scored cases is inconclusive. A person decides every proposal. The cost-monitor agent produces the weekly report and proposals. What is not measured Cloud infrastructure spend, artifact storage, engineer time and seat licences are not measured. The ledger is separate from CoFlow credits .

title: Compliance evidence pack
description: Collect CoFlow records into per-control evidence for an audit period.
text: What it is The evidence pack maps CoFlow records for an audit period to control identifiers in SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001:2022. It lists merged pull requests, a reproducible sample, exceptions, repository settings coverage, deviations and rule changes, with one page per control. Producing a pack coflow evidence-pack --input records.json --out evidence/2026-q4 The pack is a folder of Markdown and CSV files with a manifest that lists a checksum per file and a pack hash. Record the pack hash outside the folder: someone who can edit the folder can also rewrite the manifest. Text is redacted before it is written. What it does not claim It is not a certification, an attestation or an audit opinion. It does not state that any control is designed or operating effectively. Days and checks without a record are reported as “not observed”, never as compliant. Each control lists what CoFlow records cover and what must come from elsewhere. Business plan SOC 2 Type II audit support covers readiness and evidence workflows like this one. It is not a claim that CoFlow holds an issued SOC 2 report.

title: Agent Studio
description: Build, test and promote review agents that act only within limits people set.
text: Agents are flows An agent is a flow: a small graph of typed steps in three swimlanes. The people lane holds approvals and decisions, the coding tools lane holds the tools and agents that read and change code, and the CoFlow lane holds rules, checks and records. Agent Studio adds versions, a sandbox, an autonomy ladder, bindings per repository, approvals before anything leaves CoFlow, and a full run history. Agent files in a repository keep working; each maps to a default flow. You can edit a draft as a diagram, an outline or a table of steps. Agent templates CoFlow ships 17 agent templates. Each is seeded for every organization at shadow with no binding, so it does nothing until a person binds it. Agent What it does Starts on accessibility-reviewer Reviews frontend changes for labels, accessible names, roles, focus, contrast tokens and status shown by colour alone. Pull request change-control Checks that each pull request follows the change management rules before it merges. Pull request ci-cost-reviewer Reviews CI workflow changes and estimates how they move billed runner minutes. Pull request cost-monitor Reports what coding-agent work costs and proposes savings the harness has shown keep quality. Weekly or manual data-privacy-reviewer Reviews changes for personal data in logs, errors and responses, unchecked ownership and leaking tenant scopes. Pull request, nightly dependency-watch Reviews manifest and lockfile changes for unpinned versions and unreviewed new dependencies. Dependency change docs-keeper Flags documentation that no longer matches a changed route, setting, command line option or public name. Pull request incident-follow-up Checks that a revert or incident fix comes with a regression test and a lesson, and proposes the rule. Pull request migration-guard Reviews database migrations for locking, reversibility, grants and a single head. Migration change onboarding-guide Explains the standards that apply to a new contributor’s first pull request in one plain comment. Pull request performance-reviewer Reviews changes for N+1 queries, unbounded lists, missing pagination, blocking async calls and incomplete cache keys. Pull request pr-describer Checks that a pull request description says what changed, why, how it was verified and the ticket. Pull request release-readiness Checks migrations, feature flags, settings per environment and the deploy gate before a release ships. Pull request on release branches, manual security-monitor Watches every change for web security, access control and secret handling problems. Pull request, nightly standards-reviewer Reports language and framework convention findings as comments and never fails the check. Pull request test-guard Reviews test changes for network use and production data, and reports uncovered files. Pull request test-writer Proposes missing tests as a draft comment with a sketch. It never commits code. Pull request The autonomy ladder Level Runs on Outward actions Sandbox Stored test cases only None. No call to the code host. Shadow Real events None. The run records what it would have done. Assist Real events Each action only after a person approves that exact content. Auto Real events Comments and check runs without a gate. Proposals, tickets and chat messages still need a person. A run executes at the most restrictive of its pinned level, its binding’s level and the level published now, so a demotion applies to runs already in flight. Promotion moves one level at a time. Demotion is immediate and needs no approval. A kill switch pauses one agent or every agent in the organization. Paused runs stop before their next outward action. The ceiling no setting can lift No agent can merge, approve a pull request, push, force-push or bypass a check. These are refused as a step kind, an action, a level and a policy detail, and a flow that contains one does not load. No autonomy level, approval policy, policy profile or break-glass decision changes this. See agent safety . Versions and promotion evidence A draft can change. Publishing freezes it and needs a valid flow and a passing sandbox run on the exact content. Above shadow, publishing also needs an approval from someone other than the last editor. Promotion to shadow needs a passing sandbox run. Promotion to assist and auto also needs a harness run whose precision and recall meet the agent’s thresholds, and an approval under the promotion policy. A policy can also require a minimum shadow agreement. In shadow, people mark each run’s would-be actions as agree or disagree, next to what reviewers actually did. Rollback creates a new draft from an old version. History is never changed. A diff shows steps, rule selection and budget changes. Pending actions and approvals When a run reaches a person, it stores the exact content of the action and its hash. The approver confirms the hash they saw. A decision is refused if the content changed, the action expired, the person lacks the role or started the run themselves. Edits replace the draft and record who changed it; approval then applies to the new content. Before sending, CoFlow checks the hash again. Each step has an idempotency key, so a resumed run never sends twice. Who reviews and who approves is set by approval policies for teams and organizations, with quorum and independence. See approvals . Bindings and schedules A binding attaches a published agent to a repository, optionally with paths and a branch pattern, and needs an approval. A binding can have a cron schedule; scheduled runs run at shadow at most and need the scheduled jobs to be set up. Fleet, Needs you and traces Fleet: every agent with its status, level and recent runs. Pause one with its switch, or all of them at once. Needs you: approvals, actions waiting for a person and failed runs you can retry. Traces: every run stores its step trace, findings and a cost record at every level. A person can retry a failed step without sending twice, or cancel a run. Limits in this release Studio runs on real pull requests are GitHub only. GitLab and Bitbucket get the plain review. Ticket actions need a tracker connection that does not ship yet. onboarding-guide needs the code host to report a first pull request, and its promotion stays refused until evaluations can score an explanation. Under the planned billing model , sandbox, shadow and live runs use credits.

title: Workflow Studio
description: Turn self-contained HTML prototypes into reviewed, editable workflow evidence.
text: Upload and capture Upload self-contained HTML pages and select an entry page. Playback uses an opaque-origin sandbox. Record interactions, form validation, error states and in-bundle navigation. Captures are validated and converted into workflow state graphs. Edit, review and link Relabel and annotate states or transitions, and add clearly marked manual steps. Each save creates an immutable revision. Authorized reviewers approve or reject revisions. Links to requirements and bugs pin the workflow revision, capture and source provenance. Replay and export checks Replay the trace and compare settled states. Export a Playwright test using stable locators where available. Unstable selectors are flagged with suggested test IDs. Unreviewed exports carry a warning; review them before adding them to monitoring. Evidence and isolation Replay results are client-reported, not independent server verification. Uploaded HTML is untrusted and cannot run in the application origin. The sandbox blocks many external interactions, but it is not a fully network-isolated server-side browser. Use synthetic input and avoid entering secrets into prototypes. Workflow records use organization ownership, project authorization and forced PostgreSQL RLS. Read the isolation guide .

title: Row-level security (RLS) and tenant isolation
description: How CoFlow keeps each organization’s records apart, and how it guides RLS-sensitive changes in your own application.
text: Every CoFlow table is organization-owned Every CoFlow table carries an owning organization and is protected by forced PostgreSQL row-level security. Verified identity sets the organization and authorized project scope inside each transaction. Caller-supplied tenant headers are never an authorization source, and a session without organization context sees no rows. Webhook deliveries from code hosts are matched to their organization under the same policies. Runtime requirements The API, the worker and the hosted MCP service refuse to start when their database role is a superuser, can bypass RLS or owns a protected table. The worker and the MCP service also check that the CoFlow tables exist with forced RLS before starting. Migrations run through a separate role. Existing rows are backfilled to a verified owner before activation. API, MCP and worker operations set transaction-local context, including after commits and on pooled connections. Tenant isolation of the CoFlow tables is tested through the restricted runtime role on PostgreSQL. SQLite development tests do not prove RLS behavior. Inside an organization In this release, repositories are not tied to workspace projects. Any member of an organization can read any repository’s CoFlow records in that organization. RLS in applications you build The starter library includes tenant isolation rules for PostgreSQL, and the data-privacy-reviewer agent checks for tenant scopes that leak. Add your own rules and an acceptance contract that covers allowed and denied behavior. Example rule: tenant-scoped invoice access Resolve the organization from verified identity. Set its context in the query transaction. Require project authorization. Never treat possession of an invoice ID as permission. CoFlow gives your coding agents reviewed guidance. It does not install, enable or certify RLS policies in your application. A useful acceptance checklist Tenant A can read and update its own authorized records. Tenant B cannot read, update, insert into or delete Tenant A’s records. Missing organization or project scope fails closed. Connection reuse does not keep another tenant’s context. Workers and evaluations use the same authorization boundaries as API requests. Cache, search and vocabulary results stay tenant and project scoped.

title: Organizations, roles and approvals
description: Who can sign in, what each role can do, and how approvals and audit work.
text: Membership and single sign-on People sign in through your identity provider with single sign-on, provided through WorkOS, and their access follows their membership there. Local suspension and project permissions stay authoritative. Removing someone from the organization removes what they can review or approve at once; their past decisions stay in history. Roles and permissions Built-in role templates include owner, admin, maintainer, contributor and viewer. Owners can manage policies and custom roles. In CoFlow: Reading needs organization membership. Agent drafts, test cases and sandbox runs need the integrations permission. Publishing agents, changing levels, bindings, pausing and approval decisions need the review permission, and then the approval policy decides. Reviewer groups and approval policies need the organization management permission. An agent can have its own grants (view, edit, publish, promote, bind, pause) for people or groups. Once it has one, every studio route for it needs the matching grant. Reviewers and approvers A reviewer group is a named set of people, optionally joined to an organization team. An approval policy covers one kind of decision: new rules, rule changes, retirements, deviations, finding dispositions, agent publishing, promotion, bindings, pending actions, release records and context promotion. It names reviewers and approvers, how many of each are required, whether the author may count (default no), whether reviewers and approvers must differ, when it escalates and when it expires. Policies are set for the organization and can be overridden per repository, pack and path. The most specific match wins. An organization policy can be locked; overrides can then only tighten it. Only approvals from currently eligible people on the current content count. When content changes, earlier approvals stop counting. A quorum that cannot be reached is reported as blocked. It is never lowered silently. Break glass needs an owner, a policy that allows it and a reason, and is recorded. With no stored policy, any reviewer other than the author may approve. A sole eligible author may approve, and the record marks independence as not met. Audit Every state change in Agent Studio and approvals writes a row to the organization’s access audit. Chat decisions are matched by email to an active member with the review permission; anyone else is refused, and the first decision stands. Before inviting users Confirm single sign-on, the first owner, reviewer groups and approval policies. Test with two organizations, including access revocation and cross-tenant denial.

title: Agent safety and security monitoring
description: The limits every agent runs under, and the agents that watch for security problems.
text: The autonomy ceiling No CoFlow agent can merge, approve a pull request, push, force-push or bypass a check, at any level and under any policy. Autonomous pipelines stop at a draft pull request; people mark it ready and merge it. See the autonomy ladder . Deny list for coding agents CoFlow’s workflow templates install agent settings that deny force pushes, hard resets, recursive deletes, skipping commit hooks and merging pull requests, so a prompt that drifts still cannot do them. Subagents get the fewest tools and return one structured result. coflow workflows install installs the templates and coflow workflows check reports drift. Mined text is data Review comments, tickets, transcripts and incident text are treated as data, never instructions. Secrets are detected and dropped, identifiers are replaced, and instruction-like markers are neutralized before text reaches the lessons pipeline or a model. Security monitoring agents security-monitor : web security, access control and secret handling on every change, and nightly. data-privacy-reviewer : personal data in logs and responses, unchecked ownership and leaking tenant scopes. dependency-watch : unpinned versions and unreviewed new dependencies. migration-guard : locking, reversibility and grants in database migrations. They start at shadow, like every template. The Claude Code plugin also ships read-only reviewer and security-monitor subagents. Tools and credentials Tool adapters never run project code and pass no caller credential to the tool. The hosted MCP server takes identity only from the verified token. A tool input that names an organization, user or agent is refused. Configuration stores references to where a credential lives, never the value. Operational sources are read only. CoFlow never mutes a monitor, resolves an issue or acknowledges a page.

title: Connect CoFlow to your tools
description: What each integration does, and whether it is shipped, configuration-gated or not yet verified against a live account.
text: Integrations at a glance Integration What it does Status Coding agents Rule files and MCP for 12 clients Shipped; runs locally MCP server and CLI Local stdio server and hosted HTTP server Local shipped; hosted is configuration-gated GitHub Pull request review, check runs, Agent Studio runs Configuration-gated; not yet verified against a live account GitLab, Bitbucket Cloud Merge and pull request review, statuses, backfill Configuration-gated; not yet verified against a live account; no studio runs Jira, Linear Tickets as evidence and as the authorization record for a change Configuration-gated; agent ticket actions not ready Slack, Microsoft Teams Approval cards, scorecards and run messages Configuration-gated; not yet verified against a live account Datadog, Sentry, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, CloudWatch Incidents and errors as evidence Configuration-gated; not yet verified against a live account Scheduled jobs Weekly, nightly and frequent background work Operator creates the jobs Verify before you rely on it Integrations marked as not yet verified were built and tested against recorded fakes. Treat the first repository, workspace or source as a test, and check each step with your onboarding contact. A stored connection alone does not prove an integration is active. Platform connections The platform also has organization-owned GitHub and Jira connection flows through Nango, and an MCP configuration catalog that versions, reviews and audits MCP server descriptors. An approved descriptor starts disabled and does not launch a process or connect to a server.

title: Coding agents
description: One command gives a coding agent your rules, the CoFlow MCP server and correction capture.
text: coflow connect coflow connect <client> --dry-run coflow connect <client> Rule files: written from .coflow/rules/ and kept current by coflow export . MCP server: a coflow entry merged into the client’s project MCP file. Other servers and settings stay as they were. Correction capture: with --capture , a session-end hook where the client has one. Running it twice changes nothing. A file CoFlow cannot merge safely is left untouched and named in the error. Useful flags: --all , --dry-run , --hosted , --capture and --no-rules . Supported clients Client Name Rules MCP Capture Claude Code claude Skills per pack and an AGENTS.md block .mcp.json Session-end hook Cursor cursor Cursor rules per pack .cursor/mcp.json Stop hook VS Code and GitHub Copilot vscode Copilot instructions, path-scoped per pack .vscode/mcp.json coflow lesson Codex codex AGENTS.md block .codex/config.toml (trusted projects) coflow lesson Gemini CLI gemini GEMINI.md block .gemini/settings.json Session-end hook Windsurf windsurf Windsurf rules, per pack by glob User file; entry printed coflow lesson Cline cline Cline rules, per pack by path User file; entry printed coflow lesson Zed zed .rules block User settings; entry printed coflow lesson JetBrains AI Assistant jetbrains AI Assistant rules file IDE settings only coflow lesson Amazon Q Developer amazonq Amazon Q rules file .amazonq/mcp.json (local only) coflow lesson Roo Code roo Roo rules file .roo/mcp.json (local only) coflow lesson Aider aider CONVENTIONS.md block None; Aider has no MCP client coflow lesson Merged files change only between CoFlow’s start and end markers. Each format was checked against the client’s own documentation on November 19, 2026. A few details could not be confirmed there: the Roo Code and Amazon Q MCP file layouts, multiple Windsurf globs, and the transcript layout the Cursor and Gemini CLI hooks read. Check them on your client. Hosted connection and secrets connect never writes a token. A hosted connection names the COFLOW_API_TOKEN environment variable in the form each client expands when it starts; set it in your shell. Amazon Q Developer, Roo Code and Cline have no documented way to send an environment variable as a header, so --hosted refuses them; connect the local server. Capturing corrections The capture hook reads the session transcript, keeps the sentences in which a person corrected the agent, drops any that contain a secret or an instruction-like marker, and appends them to .coflow/inbox/ . It makes no network call and never fails the client. Elsewhere, record a correction with coflow lesson . A captured correction is evidence, not a rule. Claude Code plugin The Claude Code plugin packages the MCP server, the /standards , /lesson and /qa commands, read-only reviewer and security-monitor subagents and the capture hook. There is no VS Code extension; coflow connect vscode is the whole setup for Copilot.

title: MCP server and CLI
description: The local stdio server for one developer, the hosted HTTP server for teams and cloud agents, and the coflow command.
text: Local MCP server The local server runs over stdio from the repository and needs no account or token. It serves fifteen tools: five rule tools (including get_standards , get_rule , record_outcome and propose_rule ), eight context tools (including where_is and remember ), get_budget and record_cost . coflow connect configures it. Hosted MCP server The hosted server speaks streamable HTTP at /mcp . It is off by default and always requires authorization. Credentials: agent credentials created in the app, re-checked on every request against expiry, revocation and the creator’s active membership. Credentials must be organization-wide. Scopes: read access for get_standards , list_rules , get_rule and connection_status ; write access for record_outcome and propose_rule . There is no approve tool. Rules: come from the rules a repository synced with coflow sync . With that source, get_rule is not offered. Budgets: calls are limited per person and per organization, per minute and per day, and input and output sizes are bounded. A limit returns a structured error with a retry time. Logging: one line per call with the tool, a hash of the organization, duration and outcome. Arguments and results are never logged. Run one instance in this release: budgets are kept in process memory. Proposals are limited to five open per repository. MCP tool calls never use credits. Client configuration Keep the token in an environment variable. For Claude Code: { "mcpServers": { "coflow": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${COFLOW_MCP_TOKEN}" } } } } Use the address your onboarding contact gives you. coflow connect --hosted writes the equivalent entry for supported clients. The coflow command Command What it does init , scan , validate Install packs for the detected stack, show detection, validate rule files compile , export Print the rules for paths; write agent files, or check them for drift check , tools Review a diff; list tool adapters and versions connect , lesson , inbox Set up coding agents; record and list corrections context , search Work with project memory; find rules by meaning or keyword agents , workflows Manage agent files; install and check agent workflow templates sync Post the repository’s rules and context to the hosted service eval , cost Run evaluations; report costs, budgets and savings ops , evidence-pack Test operational sources; write an audit evidence pack github , gitlab , bitbucket Code host commands such as evidence backfill coflow --help lists every option.

title: GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket
description: Pull request review on the three supported code hosts, and what differs between them.
text: What each host gets GitHub GitLab Bitbucket Cloud Review result Check run named CoFlow, or one edited comment Commit status and one merge request note Build status and a comment Agent Studio runs Yes No, plain review only No, plain review only Host checks Yes Yes; some report “not available on GitLab” Yes; some read by the nightly snapshot Evidence backfill Yes Yes Yes Live account verified Not yet Not yet Not yet GitHub Connect through a GitHub App or through Nango, not both, or every event arrives twice. CoFlow needs checks write access to publish its check run; without it, the review is posted as one comment edited in place, and without either it is stored but not shown. An operator confirms a GitHub App installation before it routes deliveries. Deliveries forwarded by Nango are routed by connection. GitLab Works with gitlab.com and self-managed GitLab. Webhooks for merge requests become queued jobs, answered with a CoFlow commit status and one note from the bot user. Approval rules are read only on GitLab tiers that have them, and protection for administrators has no GitLab setting, so that host check always reports “not available”. Bitbucket Cloud Bitbucket Cloud pull requests get a build status and a comment. Bitbucket Data Center is not covered. Your first repository All three hosts were built and tested against recorded fakes. Treat the first repository as a test: open a pull request, confirm the delivery is accepted, check that the result appears on the host, then push a new commit and confirm it updates.

title: Jira, Linear, Slack and Teams
description: Tickets as evidence and authorization, and approvals in chat.
text: Jira and Linear CoFlow reads Jira and Linear tickets as evidence for lessons and as the authorization record for a change: the ticket a pull request names. Incident priorities mark a ticket as an incident. Ticket text is data, never instructions. Opening a ticket from an agent is not ready in this release. An approved ticket action fails with a note, and nothing is sent. Slack and Microsoft Teams CoFlow posts proposed rules, weekly scorecards, agent run messages and assigned approvals to chat. A reviewer can approve or reject a proposed rule on the card. The person who clicks is matched to a CoFlow user by email and must be an active member with the review permission. The person who proposed a rule cannot decide it. The first decision stands; a later click shows it. Approving in chat records the decision only. The rule becomes active when its pull request is merged, and every card says so. A chat message from an agent is sent at most once. If a worker stops between sending and recording, the next attempt does not resend. Setup Each chat app is installed for your workspace by an administrator with the app’s own secrets. Neither the Slack nor the Teams app has been verified against a live workspace yet; send a test message first.

title: Datadog, Sentry, PagerDuty, Opsgenie and CloudWatch
description: Production incidents and errors as evidence for new rules, read only.
text: What CoFlow reads Source Reads Becomes Datadog Error tracking issues, monitors that alerted, APM error spans, deployment events Error and alert evidence; deploy markers Sentry Issues, in-app frame paths of the latest event, releases Error evidence; release markers PagerDuty Incidents and the kind and time of each log entry Incident evidence Opsgenie Incidents and the kind and time of each timeline entry Incident evidence AWS CloudWatch Alarms that moved into ALARM, and one aggregate Logs Insights query you configure Alert and error evidence CoFlow only reads. It never mutes a monitor, resolves an issue, acknowledges a page or changes an alarm. These integrations have not been verified against live accounts yet. Linking errors to changes A signal is linked to a pull request only when a release or deployment marker names it. Other signals after a deploy are candidates: a spike against the count before the deploy, an error group first seen after it, or an incident inside the window. Correlation is not causation; only a marker counts a signal as an escaped defect. Setup Configuration names where each credential lives, never the credential; a value that looks like a credential is refused. coflow ops test checks each source and its read access without printing a secret, and coflow ops policy prints the AWS read policy. A scheduled job reads new items every hour. What is never collected Credential values. Request bodies, query strings, headers, cookies and local variables. User IDs, names, emails, IP addresses and session IDs. Messages are turned into templates first. Raw log lines, event payloads, responder names and timeline comments. Monitor queries, alarm reasons and metric values.

title: Scheduled jobs
description: Background work that runs only after an operator creates the jobs.
text: The jobs Job Suggested schedule What it does Weekly scorecard Mondays Posts the weekly scorecard to each organization’s chosen chat channels Host snapshots Nightly Takes a host settings snapshot of every bound repository Approvals Every 15 minutes Escalates or expires open approval requests and tells the fallback group once Pending actions Every 10 minutes Expires pending agent actions and advances runs left waiting Stale facts Weekly Flags learned facts that are unverified, unconfirmed and older than 90 days Retention Monthly Deletes old job ledger rows (default 180 days, minimum 30). Nothing else Ops ingest Hourly Reads new incidents and errors and links them to merged or deployed pull requests Agent schedules Every minute Starts Agent Studio runs whose binding schedule is due, at shadow at most Every job is safe to run twice and prints one result line per organization. Nothing runs on a schedule until an operator creates the jobs; until then the weekly scorecard, snapshots, escalation and expiry, stale facts, retention, ops ingest and agent schedules do not happen. Getting started In the first week of a pilot, a single daily job that runs all of them in order is enough, at the cost of slower escalation and expiry. Each job uses the worker’s environment and the restricted database role.

title: Troubleshooting
description: Start with the boundary that is blocking the workflow.
text: I can sign in but cannot open a project Have an administrator check active local membership, current provider membership, project assignment and project status. Provider login is not enough. Do not work around the issue by adding a tenant ID to a request header. Compilation is blocked Read the blocker and selection reasons. Check approved rule revisions, declared conflict groups, pinned dependency status and required instruction size. Resolve the source issue and compile a new package; historical packages remain immutable. Rows disappear after enabling RLS Confirm ownership backfill and transaction-local organization plus authorized project scope. Use the correct restricted runtime role. Verify PostgreSQL behavior in a disposable environment before rollout; do not disable production policies to make a query return rows. An integration or module is unavailable Check that the exact deployed release contains the feature, its flags are enabled, and the provider/worker configuration is complete. A stored connection or catalog entry alone does not prove an adapter is active. Ask for help Send the module, safe error code, approximate time and deployed version to support@getcoflow.ai . Share package IDs only through an approved support channel. Do not include tokens, personal data or private source content.
